newsitem.title: GABON: Mbeki takes Zaire talks invitation to Mobutu.
newsitem.headline: Mbeki takes Zaire talks invitation to Mobutu.

text.p: South African Vice-President Thabo Mbeki headed towards a meeting with Zaire President Mobutu Sese Seko in Gabon on Saturday carrying an invitation for talks with rebel leader Laurent Kabila, officials said.
"Mbeki will meet with Gabon's President Omar Bongo and then Mobutu, the two meetings are likely to take around one and three quarter hours," said one South African official in Libreville.
On Friday, Mbeki said he had won a commitment from Kabila, whose fighters have reached the approaches to the capital Kinshasa, to give diplomacy a chance.

Bill Richardson, U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, said he still believed a peaceful transition in Zaire was possible but that any new government would "most likely" be headed by Kabila in light of his military victories.
He said that the transitional phase should include various factions. "The big issue is going to be how much of Mobutu's people, if any at all, are part of that," he said.
Mbeki said Kabila had agreed to meet Mobutu on a South African ship on Wednesday for their second round of face-to-face talks and he assumed Mobutu would also agree to attend.
Richardson also said a peaceful handover would require another face-to-face meeting between Kabila and Mobutu "probably in the Congo" in the middle of next week.

"A lot of posturing takes place," he said in a television interview. "I believe that Mobutu will return to Kinshasa before he heads for the Congo. I believe he is putting his affairs in order. But eventually I do believe there's still a good chance of a peaceful inclusive transition government."
A first ship-borne session between the civil war foes hosted by South Africa's Nelson Mandela ended inconclusively last weekend.
Mobutu's son Nzanga said the president would return to Kinshasa on Saturday after the talks with Mbeki.
"People outside (Zaire) are saying that President Mobutu will go into exile. This is to bring panic. They do not know the president," Mobutu Nzanga told Reuters.

Rebels said they had pushed Mobutu's army 50 km (30 miles) beyond their previous outpost at Kenge, 200 km (125 miles) east of Kinshasa in heavy fighting. It was not clear when the fighting took place.
It was not possible to verify the rebel claims, which in the past have often proved false.
Rebel "foreign minister" Bizima Karaha told Reuters Angolan UNITA troops, who fought a 20-year civil war against the government with backing from Washington and Mobutu, were helping the Zaire army.
Western intelligence sources say Angola, and Zaire's eastern neighbours Uganda and Rwanda give military help to Kabila.
Richardson said the Angolans needed "to step aside...They've got, unfortunately, some negative intentions in terms of moving their troops into Zaire to pay back Mobutu."
Mobutu, 66, dominated the mineral-rich country at the heart of Africa for more than three decades until prostate cancer and the rebellion, launched in October, loosened his hold.
In Gabon, he met several French-speaking African presidents who urged Zaire's parliament to play a role in ending the war.
But Karaha rejected the plan of hand, describing the proposal as "absolute nonsense" and said Mobutu would be chased away if he was still in Kinshasa when rebels arrived.
Karaha demanded that power should be handed directly to "President" Kabila.
In seven months, the rebels, initially a small force fighting for the nationality of ethnic Tutsis, have won control of around three quarters of the vast country.

Richardson warned Kabila that he needed to make sure his troops stopped mistreating Rwandan Hutu refugees and punished those responsible for refugee massacres in eastern Zaire if he wanted respect from the international community.
"He is going to need private investment and international assistance to survive, because literally Zaire right at this moment is falling apart," Richardson said.
But without waiting for a peace agreement, American, Canadian and other Western companies have been making deals with Kabila for mining rights in the areas he controls.
